one_line: Nick Heiner (Surge AI) on why benchmarks drift from real value (cost, contamination, reward hacking, bad verifiers, leaderboard gaming) and how to build better ones.
summary: Heiner argues that benchmarks often diverge from real-world value because of incentives and poor methodology, and that the industry's reliance on popular but weak benchmarks (LM Arena, SWE-bench Verified, IFEval, Apex, Automation Bench) feeds a popularity loop. He lists anti-patterns: high build cost that pushes teams toward cheap or AI-assisted task creation, contamination through memorized public Q&A, reward hacking by lazy optimizers, and verifiers that reject valid answers (hard-coded string matches, contradictory or impossible prompts, Unicode look-alike tricks). He describes benchmaxxing from the lab side, including hill-climbing while human eval stays flat, crowd voting on LM Arena via watermarks, and undisclosed testing of many models. His recipe for a good benchmark is expert humans with product sense, real input data, working tools, two-way alignment between prompts and verifiers, thorough QC, and a private holdout set. He also says saturation can hide broken tasks, which adds noise to rankings, and presents Surge's Hemingway-Bench, which uses blind comparisons by professional writers instead of an LLM judge. The talk is partly a hiring pitch, but it has concrete, checkable failure cases.

key_ideas.idea: Benchmarks become a popularity feedback loop
key_ideas.detail: Because everyone needs a way to pick models but few can judge whether a benchmark is good, people judge by popularity. That shifts the conversation toward incumbency and marketing rather than real-world value.

key_ideas.idea: Building a good benchmark is expensive, so teams cut corners
key_ideas.detail: Speaker's estimate: 1,000 coding tasks at 60 hours each with $500k/yr engineers is about $15M, and roughly a third of tasks go stale each year as models improve. Workarounds like AI-written tasks or cheap labor produce weak results. Quality needs paid expert humans.

key_ideas.idea: Contamination is the default unless you work hard against it
key_ideas.detail: Public questions and answers get memorized. Given the first part of an SWE-bench Verified prompt, a model reproduced the rest verbatim, and the speaker's team found memorization above the rest of the source repos. The model card did not disclose this.

key_ideas.idea: Design verifiers against a maximally lazy optimizer
key_ideas.detail: Reward hacking is meeting the letter but not the spirit of a task. Gradient descent follows the path of least resistance, so verifiers must hold up against that pressure.

key_ideas.idea: Verifiers that reject valid answers make benchmarks useless
key_ideas.detail: Hard-coded string matches fail when many formats are acceptable, such as phone numbers. In Automation Bench, Haiku and Fable both score 20%, but for different reasons (one makes mistakes, the other picks a different valid format), so the task does not separate them. IFEval has contradictory or unsolvable prompts and a weak sentence splitter, and a response could pass by using a Cyrillic I instead of an ASCII I.

key_ideas.idea: Hill-climbing can diverge from human preference, and arenas can be gamed
key_ideas.detail: A benchmark can keep rising while human eval stays flat or falls. Leaderboards with little voter filtering can be manipulated with watermarks that tell a crowd which anonymized model to vote for. Undisclosed testing of many variants (the talk cites Meta testing 27 models) distorts results.

key_ideas.idea: Benchmark quality needs experts, real data, working tools, two-way verifier alignment, and a holdout
key_ideas.detail: Experts with product sense decide the task types and success criteria. Input data should come from the real world. Every prompt requirement needs a verifier, and every verifier check needs a prompt requirement. Keep a private holdout set. Saturation at about 80% can mean 20% of tasks are broken, and those broken tasks bias the ranking.

key_ideas.idea: Subjective quality needs blind expert comparisons, not mechanical metrics or an LLM judge
key_ideas.detail: For writing, Surge built Hemingway-Bench with thousands of professional writers doing blind pairwise model comparisons. The speaker argues LLM judges lack good taste, so they cannot expand the frontier from within it.

techniques.name: Two-way verifier-prompt alignment audit
techniques.how: Check that every requirement in the prompt is covered by a verifier, and that every verifier check corresponds to something the prompt asks for. Fix either gap before trusting scores.
techniques.when: Whenever you write or review an eval task, especially tool-call or instruction-following tasks.

techniques.name: Accept all valid answer formats in verifiers
techniques.how: Normalize or allow multiple equivalent forms (phone formats, date formats) instead of one hard-coded string match. Otherwise correct models get penalized.
techniques.when: When graders compare strings for entities that have many valid surface forms.

techniques.name: Adversarial check of graders against lazy solutions
techniques.how: Probe a grader with cheap exploits, such as look-alike Unicode characters or outputs that satisfy a count check without doing the task, and confirm they fail.
techniques.when: Before using any automated grader, and especially any grader used as a training reward.

techniques.name: Contamination probe by prefix completion
techniques.how: Give the model the first part of a benchmark item and check whether it reproduces the hidden remainder, including the reference answer, verbatim. Compare against matched non-benchmark text from the same source.
techniques.when: Before trusting public benchmark scores, or when building a benchmark from public repos or Q&A.

techniques.name: Private holdout plus disclosure of test conditions
techniques.how: Keep a private test split that is never published. Report the number of variants tested and the eval conditions.
techniques.when: When you publish or rely on leaderboard-style results.

techniques.name: Watch for benchmark-vs-human-eval divergence
techniques.how: Track a benchmark alongside a human rating set. A flat or falling human score while the benchmark rises is a sign of overfitting.
techniques.when: During iterative model or prompt tuning against a proxy metric.

techniques.name: Blind pairwise expert comparison for subjective quality
techniques.how: Have domain experts compare anonymized outputs side by side and build a leaderboard from the results. Use it where mechanical metrics and LLM judges are not trusted.
techniques.when: For writing, taste, or other quality dimensions that do not reduce to a string or a rubric.

techniques.name: Saturation check for broken tasks
techniques.how: When a benchmark plateaus, audit the failing tasks for broken verifiers or impossible prompts before concluding the model is at its limit.
techniques.when: When a benchmark score stops moving, or near a high ceiling.

numbers.claim: Benchmark build cost: 1,000 tasks x 60 hours each at $500k/yr per engineer is about $15M
Yearly replacement cost is about $5M, assuming a third of tasks become obsolete each year
Automation Bench: Haiku and Fable both score 20%; Fable is said to be correct 80% of the time but picks a different valid format from the grader
Meta tested 27 models without disclosing it, which the speaker says distorted LM Arena results
Saturation near 80% can hide roughly 20% of tasks being broken

hot_takes: LM Arena may be doing more harm than good and should consider that question seriously
Contamination is the default outcome for public benchmarks unless the builder works very hard against it
LLM-as-a-judge does not work for writing quality because LLMs lack good taste
Labs are not in the habit of disclosing benchmark contamination in model cards
Most current benchmarks are not built with product sense, so they measure the wrong things

relevance.why: AgentOS plans evals (RAGAS, load tests) and an agent stack. The talk's verifier and contamination lessons apply to those evals, but nothing is specific to its architecture.
relevance.action: When writing AgentOS eval cases, check each grader for hard-coded string matches and run a prefix-completion contamination probe on any public-derived test set.

relevance.why: ProsHarness runs checks around Claude Code, so the verifier-alignment and adversarial-grader points could apply to its completion checks.
relevance.action: Audit ProsHarness completion and checkpoint verifiers for strict string matching and for any path a lazy agent could use to pass without doing the work.

relevance.why: The verifier-alignment audit, contamination probe, and holdout discipline apply to any model choice or agent evaluation the team runs.
relevance.action: Before choosing a model from a public leaderboard, run the candidate models on a small private task set with two-way verifier checks and a holdout.
